hypotheses.name: The IRGC, not Mojtaba, rules Iran (working model) — HELD 82%
hypotheses.d: HELD. The promised authenticated footage of Mojtaba meeting commanders still has not landed, so the falsifier remains un-run. The week was IRGC-forward — the Guard, not the foreign ministry, confirmed it ran the Oman channel and announced the revenue-sharing terms, and the Guard made the mine-strike claim — but that is DENIED as a raise under the shared-prediction rule: 'the Guard runs the maritime file' is predicted just as strongly by an ordinary reading in which the IRGC is a powerful institution under a functioning Supreme Leader, which is a much weaker claim than 'the IRGC rules Iran'. The 82% cap stands for exactly the reason it was set.

hypotheses.name: The Iran file is coalition-captured (the capture read, tracked as opinion)
hypotheses.d: The claim: on the Iran file, organized coalition pressure — donor networks, primary structure, allied commitments, defense-institutional momentum — outweighs the base's war fatigue, which is why a 'no more wars' White House struck anyway and now substitutes sanctions for settlement rather than sign a visible retreat before the midterms. Mechanisms named, plural: status clock vs electoral clock, sunk cost after declaring victory, lobbies as veto players that raise the price of defection (one interest group among several — any single-key version of this hypothesis is scored separately and currently rejected). Held at 70%: the strike itself, the 6-month grind, and 'not in a hurry' all fit; capped because the same facts also fit ordinary planning failure plus vanity. Falsifier: a signed de-escalation or negotiated Hormuz reopening BEFORE the midterms — the base's clock winning on the party's most captured file would kill the strong form outright.

hypotheses.name: Nobody's hurrying on Hormuz — 60% → 65% (RAISED)
hypotheses.d: Its first fact that BEATS a rival instead of merely fitting itself. On 30 Aug the US struck two IRGC rocket launchers on Larak after observing Guard personnel preparing to fire rockets carrying sea mines into the strait — two days after CENTCOM declared the lanes fully cleared, and while Muscat negotiates a minesweeping calendar. The 08-30 audit had installed a genuine rival — a physical clock, minesweeping simply takes time — and ruled this hypothesis must beat it. A physical clock runs down; this one is being rewound, by the exact actor the hypothesis named in advance. Capped at +5 on three counts kept in front: CENTCOM is the interested party and 'observed preparations' is unpublished intelligence used to justify a strike; Al Jazeera published a technical challenge on 31 Aug to whether Iran can even mine by rocket as claimed; and IRGC counter-coercion against a blockade that has redirected 83 vessels, disabled three and boarded two explains the same act without any rent motive. Not pre-event.

hypotheses.name: Détente as harvest cover — HELD 60%, tell sharpened
hypotheses.d: August continues the signature: 125 PLA aerial ADIZ incursions (the 2026 decline intact) against 152 non-warship PRC vessels in the first 21 days, ~60% coast guard, with the east-of-Taiwan patrols now a declared 'new normal'. Kinetic down, jurisdiction up. NOT moved — this is the same signal that bought +5 on 08-26, and re-marking on the continuation of its own evidence is the double-count the audit named. The important item is against my own test: if Beijing has DECLARED the patrols permanent, their persistence through the Sept 24 visit is close to uninformative. Re-specified now, in advance and stricter — the informative observation on 09-23→09-25 is a boarding, an inspection, or a first-time-area incursion. Mere presence no longer counts as confirmation.

hypotheses.name: Venezuela was a Hormuz hedge in a drug-war uniform
hypotheses.d: The clearest revealed-preference play on the board — and the reason it holds at 55 rather than higher. Sturdy mechanism first: US Gulf-Coast refineries are plumbed for heavy sour crude, Venezuela sits on the planet's largest heavy reserves, and moving that barrel north through the Caribbean to Texas and Louisiana structurally hedges the one risk that ran live all year — a Hormuz closure. The Aug 28-29 deal (a new operator taking control of ~65bn barrels, about a fifth of Venezuela's reserves) is exactly what this hypothesis predicts. So oil-as-motive is near-certain. What is NOT settled — and what caps this — is premeditation: was Southern Spear a counter-narcotics and regime-change campaign that harvested the oil after the fact, or an oil-security operation in a drug-war uniform from the start? The tell against design is the clock — the deal trailed Maduro's Jan 3 capture by eight months, which reads more like spoils than master plan. Falsifiers: token export volumes, Gulf-Coast heavy sourcing not actually swinging off the Middle East, or the fixed infrastructure (GEO-022) never appearing. One correction the excitement needs: a canal cannot bypass Hormuz — the hedge is source substitution plus Caribbean routing, not a waterway. Note it is DISTINCT from 'The Portfolio State' below, which is about the vehicle rather than the motive.

hypotheses.name: US drift hardened into leverage play — HELD 52%
hypotheses.d: Confirming but shared, therefore ambience: Treasury again held back on Chinese financial institutions, with mainstream reporting now naming the mechanism outright — designating them 'could create tensions before Xi's visit'. Bessent's promised weekly cadence hit banks but no Chinese one, and at the G20 he pushed severing Iran financial ties while China dissented. Both the leverage read and the ordinary 'Washington won't detonate its own summit' read predict all of it. The strongest weekly argument AGAINST, logged rather than absorbed: the US struck Iran on three consecutive nights and took Iranian fire onto three Arab host states. Deliberate slow-walking for leverage sits badly with sustained kinetic escalation that raises the cost of the thing being slow-walked — that counterweight is what holds the number at 52.

hypotheses.name: A pre-announcement leak into oil futures — 40% → 34% (biggest mover)
hypotheses.d: Its lead conditional has now gone unfired across three weeks containing the most violently market-moving Iran news since April — the 30 Aug Larak strike, three nights of exchanges, two struck VLCCs, Brent to ~$95 — with not one reported nine-figure pre-announcement episode. The file is confirmed as historical and bounded: DOJ is probing four trades totalling ~$2.6bn, all inside a five-week window that closed in April — Mar 23 (>$500m, ~15 min before Trump's delay post), Apr 7 ($960m before the ceasefire), Apr 17 ($760m, ~20 min before Iran said Hormuz was open), Apr 21 ($430m before the extension). CORRECTION BANKED AGAINST THIS ENTRY: the ledger's earlier '~$2.2bn cluster' for Mar 23 and its '~$7bn' aggregate are both withdrawn as over-wide constructions. The cut is made on the hypothesis's own written terms, not on a preferred reading — a conditional set at 60% has burned three of fourteen weeks in the best environment it will ever get and produced nothing. The cut is only −6 because of one genuinely new structural fact: investigators are running a SEPARATE probe into prediction-market activity on the same developments, and the same foreknowledge reaching two unrelated venues is hard to explain as one market-maker hedging client flow. Split now: deliberate leak 34 / mediator-side 20 / skilled opportunism 36 / coincidence 10. Still the only entry whose evidence is timestamped BEFORE the event.

hypotheses.name: NEW · The Portfolio State — coercion converted into sovereign equity, statute retrofitted
hypotheses.d: Strongest form: the US is converting military and sanctions leverage into permanent state equity in strategic supply chains, with the legal authority written to fit transactions rather than the reverse — Venezuela being the first hydrocarbon use of a template already run in chips and critical minerals. The rail predates the headline, which is the only thing licensing a design read at all: Senate NDAA FY2027 §1051 was marked up in MID-JUNE — ten weeks before the 29 Aug deal — creating a DoD Equity Investment Account, authorising OSC equity to $500m and capping any single position at 40% of the entity; the Venezuela stake is 35%, inside a cap that does not legally exist yet. Add DoD's own $400m/15% stake in MP Materials with 100% offtake (structurally identical to Venezuela's '20% of output at cost'), House Oversight already demanding an accounting of Venezuelan oil revenue on 23 Feb, and CFR's tally of 26 government equity deals worth ~$23.9bn. It opens at only 25% because the boring, incompetence and patronage readings are all strong: think tanks have been publicly naming and counting this pattern since 2025 (a policy, not a plot); the Pentagon's own spokesman flatly DENIES that OSC takes equity while WSJ reports it doing so, which is improvisation not design; and a 100-year concession over 65bn bbl routed to one politically connected operator with no published contract is better explained as spoils allocation. Above all the base rate is enormous — Anglo-Persian 1914, the RFC, GM/Chrysler 2009 — so the design premium must be small. NOT a conspiracy claim and must never be scored as one: it requires no secrecy at all, only anticipation, and the honest gap is that I cannot name the operator who executes the warrants. Key test: does the ENACTED NDAA widen §1051 beyond critical minerals to energy, or raise the cap, by 31 Dec (45%)? Scope enacted unchanged kills the design read.

hypotheses.name: Moscow shapes Tehran's maximalism — 25% → 22% (CUT, sixth session running)
hypotheses.d: The week finally produced Russia-Iran material and it is the wrong KIND. Moscow said publicly on 01 Sep that air defence is the main focus of military-technical cooperation with Iran, alongside a reported 500 Verba MANPADS and 2,500 missiles and continued fighter deliveries. That is the resupply leg — already priced at 7/10 under 'means'. It moves nothing: it is announced by TASS, an interested party publishing its own helpfulness and the structural opposite of a covert channel; the opportunism branch predicts arms sales to a client at war identically, so under the standing rule it is ambience; and after six sessions there is still ZERO documentary evidence Moscow has influenced Tehran's negotiating position, which is the actual claim. Arms transfers are not persuasion. Cut rather than held because a decay rule that bites only on its deadline is a cliff, not decay. Clock unchanged: 15% on 30 Sep absent documentary evidence, retire below 10%.

hypotheses.name: War pause was secretly packaged with the Beijing summit — on the retirement line
hypotheses.d: Nothing resolved this week, and one file addition cuts against it: the summit's Iran content is now openly reported as an explicit US ask — Chinese pressure on Tehran to reopen the strait — with Beijing expected to want Taiwan concessions in return. An openly negotiated Iran-for-Taiwan trade is this hypothesis's RIVAL, not its confirmation; the secret-package version needs the deal hidden, and the deal is being conducted in headlines. Retirement trigger unchanged; the test runs on schedule on 24 Sept.

brief.head: Bahrain refuses Iran's Hormuz talks as US says its blockade is airtight
brief.h: Bahrain's foreign ministry said it 'will not participate' in Monday's Iran-proposed meeting in Oman on safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz, hours before US Central Command said its forces had redirected 100 commercial vessels in the 60 days since the blockade of Iranian ports resumed and that 'ZERO ships' had passed without US permission.
brief.t: There are now two blockades in the same water, and Monday's meeting is a contest over which one gets written down. Iran's version is a permit regime - Tehran's spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei calls the meeting 'a sign of Iran's good intention' and says delegations will be briefed on the Iran-Oman consultations on passage - while Washington's version is a naval cordon around Iran's own ports, and CENTCOM chose today to publish its scorecard. Bahrain's refusal is the tell: Manama, which hosts the US Fifth Fleet and has had no diplomatic relations with Tehran since 2016, says the strait must stay open without 'discrimination, fees or permits'. Sitting in a room where Iran briefs its passage terms is the first step to those terms becoming the practice, and the one Gulf state whose security is literally headquartered in the US Navy declined to take it.
brief.context: EPOCH: the 1987-88 Tanker War, when the US reflagged and escorted Kuwaiti tankers for fourteen months rather than negotiate transit terms with Iran - the precedent that a Gulf transit regime is set by who escorts, not by who hosts a meeting. CONSTRAINT: Iran's leverage is the closure and its only way to monetise it is formalisation - fees, permits, an administrator - while the US blockade denies Iran the revenue that would make a long closure affordable; each side's instrument exists to break the other's. DESK: in Tehran the Supreme National Security Council and the Revolutionary Guards navy decide passage, so the foreign ministry's meeting is the diplomatic wrapper; in Manama the royal court decides, and on this question it moves with Riyadh and Washington. BASE RATE: Bahrain has broken ranks with Saudi Arabia on Iran almost never since the 2011 Peninsula Shield deployment, so its absence is expected; the informative attendance list is the one that has not been published - whether Riyadh, Abu Dhabi, Doha and Kuwait send ministers, and at what level. Al Jazeera reports no signed agreement is expected. CENTCOM's 'ZERO ships' figure is the command's own count and has no independent tally behind it in today's reporting. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: any Gulf state accepting a passage fee or permit language in writing, which moves GEO-013 toward the top of its range; a named neutral administrator with no Iranian role moves it down.

angles.effect: Gains the look of the reasonable neighbour and a room of Gulf delegations hearing its passage terms, which is how a permit regime becomes customary - without conceding the closure
Buys alignment credit with Washington and Riyadh by refusing to legitimise permits, and pays in being first in line if Iran wants to show that non-attendees get worse terms
Publishes a clean number that frames the US cordon as the working regime; the cost is that it advertises the blockade is also why Gulf supply stays tight
Pay under both regimes at once - rerouting, war-risk insurance and cargo that cannot move through either gate

dec.kill: The published attendance and outcome of Monday's Oman meeting: a joint text that mentions fees, permits or an Iranian administrator kills the 'Bahrain is the Gulf norm' read; Saudi Arabia and the UAE also staying away kills the 'meeting as recognition' read from the other side.

consp.claim: That the United States could retake the Strait of Hormuz in 24 hours if it wanted to, so the continued closure is a deliberate choice serving someone's balance sheet - and CENTCOM's boast that no ship passes without US permission is read as proof that Washington, not Tehran, is really running the strait.
consp.spread: A running /pol/ thread and a line repeated constantly inside the Persia-Israel general (/pig/ #2121 today), with the CENTCOM 'ZERO ships' post circulating on X.
consp.read: A capability claim smuggling an intent claim. The kernel is literally true in one narrow sense - the US does control what enters and leaves Iranian ports - but that is a cordon around Iran, not an open strait for everyone else, and clearing mines and dispersed anti-ship batteries is measured in weeks. What survives is the fair question of who profits from a long closure, which is analysis rather than conspiracy.

brief.head: Iraq shuts three Iran crossings after drone launchers found near border
brief.h: Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi closed the Shalamcheh, al-Shib and Mandali crossings after security forces found drone launch platforms in the remote al-Tib area of Maysan, near the Iranian frontier, and approved Iran's request for a joint investigation into the attack that shut Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline.
brief.t: The important thing is who is paying to stay out of this. Baghdad has now sacked its Maysan commander, closed the border posts the launchers sat beside, and described the closure as an economic measure - and Tehran, the presumed patron, asked to investigate alongside it. That is a host state and a patron both building a paper trail that says 'not us', which is exactly what you do when the alternative is becoming someone else's target set. Follow the money: those crossings carry Iranian goods, fuel and pilgrims into a country that buys Iranian gas and electricity, so Iraq is taxing its own trade to avoid a bill from Washington and Riyadh. The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, meanwhile, called the strike 'an honour that we do not claim' - praise without a signature, the classic grammar of deniability.
brief.context: EPOCH: a late chapter of the post-2003 settlement in which Iraq became a state whose army, parliament and militias answer to different patrons; the Popular Mobilization Forces were folded into the state payroll in 2016 without being folded into its chain of command. CONSTRAINT: Baghdad cannot disarm the groups that launch from its soil without a civil fight it would likely lose, so it does the next-cheapest thing - it closes gates and fires commanders, which punishes geography rather than organizations. DESK: the decisions that matter are made by the Prime Minister's office on the border, by OFAC on whether to name a group and its money, and by CENTCOM on whether a launch site ever becomes a strike target; the Iraqi parliament's speaker rejecting the use of Iraqi territory is narration, not an instrument. BASE RATE: after the 2019 Abqaiq attack and the militia strikes of 2019-20, the modal outcome was designations and air-defence deployments, with kinetic US strikes in Iraq following only after American casualties. INCOMPETENCE ALTERNATIVE: a border that leaks drones is a border that leaks everything, and the simplest reading is a porous frontier plus a militia acting without a plan, not a coordinated Iranian escalation. FALSIFIER: the crossings reopen within a week with no named group and no Treasury action - that would say today was theatre for Riyadh. Our wire on Iraq becoming a target set stays armed; nothing today fired it.

angles.effect: Buys distance from the attack by closing its own trade routes - it pays in customs revenue, fuel and pilgrim traffic to avoid paying in sanctions or strikes
Asking to join the investigation lets it look like a victim of rogue actors while keeping the militia network intact; the joint probe also gives it eyes on what Iraq finds
Gets visible Iraqi action without having to retaliate, which is what it promised not to do - but its pipeline is still shut
Pay first and most, with no reopening date announced

dec.kill: A US Treasury designation naming the specific Iraqi group and its financial network, or recovered airframes traced to Iranian production, would turn 'drones from Iraq' into an evidential finding. Crossings reopening quietly within a week with no name would say the closure was a gesture.

consp.claim: That Saudi oil exports have already gone to zero and the figure is being hidden, and that the pipeline is wrecked for six to twelve months, so 150-dollar oil is locked in whatever Baghdad does.
consp.spread: The 'SAUDI OIL EXPORTS DROPPED TO 0' thread on /pol/ has passed 175 replies, and '150 dollar oil soon' threads are running on /biz/ citing satellite fire detections along the pipeline route.
consp.read: The kernel is real - Saudi crude supply fell about 2.3 million barrels a day in August to roughly 6 million - but the jump from a precautionary shutdown to a destroyed line has no engineering source behind it. Brent actually settled DOWN 2.8 per cent on Friday at $104.61 on news of Gulf-Iran talks, which is not how a market prices a permanent loss.

brief.head: Zelensky offers to meet Putin at Miami G20; Kremlin says only Moscow
brief.h: Volodymyr Zelensky told Deutsche Welle he would 'of course' meet Vladimir Putin at the G20 summit in Miami on 14-15 December, and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov answered from New Delhi that it is 'impossible' while 'there is a readiness to meet him in Moscow'.
brief.t: The argument is about the room, because the room is the concession. A meeting on a US-hosted G20 stage puts Zelensky beside Putin as an equal head of state under Washington's roof; a meeting in Moscow makes the Ukrainian president the visitor to the capital that invaded him, which is why the Kremlin keeps offering it and Kyiv keeps refusing it. That makes Zelensky's offer nearly costless - he knows the answer - and its real audience is Washington, where he is due to see Trump in late September after Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff shuttled between Moscow and Kyiv and Trump and Putin spoke by phone this week. Being the party that said yes is currency with a US president who wants a deal.
brief.context: EPOCH: the last Putin-Zelensky meeting was the Normandy Format summit in Paris in December 2019; every leader-level offer since 2022 has died on sequencing, with Moscow insisting a meeting can only ratify terms already agreed and Kyiv wanting a meeting to negotiate them. CONSTRAINT: Putin attending a G20 on US soil is itself unconfirmed, and a Moscow venue is a precondition dressed as an invitation. DESK: in Moscow only Putin decides and Peskov is the thermostat; in Kyiv the Presidential Office and chief negotiator Rustem Umerov carry the file; in Washington the Kushner-Witkoff channel, not the State Department, is the operative desk. BASE RATE: every direct Russia-Ukraine negotiating round since the invasion has met in a third country - Belarus and Istanbul in 2022, Istanbul again in 2025 - never in either capital. Zelensky's claim that Ukraine is 'much stronger than last year on the battlefield' is his framing, stated as Russian strikes are forecast to cut up to 1.5 points off Ukrainian GDP this year. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: a Kremlin confirmation that Putin will go to Miami, or Peskov naming a third-country venue - either is stage A of the ladder this desk is already tracking.

angles.effect: Banks the image of the willing party with Trump ahead of their late-September meeting, at almost no risk because the refusal was predictable
Keeps its venue precondition and spends nothing; pays only if Washington starts reading 'Moscow only' as the obstacle
Gets a possible showpiece for its own G20 presidency, and carries the embarrassment if Putin's attendance becomes the story instead
Pay for the stalemate over venue in another winter of strikes on energy and industry

dec.kill: Peskov or Ushakov confirming Putin's attendance at Miami, or proposing a neutral third-country venue; a repeat of 'Moscow only' after Zelensky's Trump meeting keeps this read intact.

brief.head: Anthropic ties AI influence campaign on Sudan to UAE officials
brief.h: Anthropic said on 11 September it had disrupted an operation it linked 'with high confidence' to UAE government officials that used its Claude model to run roughly 300 fake social media accounts, compile 'counter-accountability dossiers' on UN special rapporteurs critical of the UAE's role in Sudan, and ghost-write testimony for the 62nd session of the UN Human Rights Council under a borrowed Sudanese rights group's name.
brief.t: The target tells you where the pressure on Abu Dhabi actually comes from. The UAE has repeatedly been accused of arming the Rapid Support Forces in a war that has killed more than 200,000 people, which it denies; the accountability rail on that charge runs through UN rapporteurs and the Human Rights Council, so the reported operation went at the rail itself - dossiers on the investigators and 'independent local witnesses' who were in fact state messaging. The ideological wrapper is the older story: the operation's AI persona, 'Deadshot', was steered by a doctrine to 'dismantle the Muslim Brotherhood globally', the frame Abu Dhabi has used since 2013 to cast Sudan's army-aligned camp as Islamists and itself as the bulwark. Anthropic says it cannot tell whether any of the testimony reached the Council or changed anything.
brief.context: DISCLOSURE: this desk runs on Claude, Anthropic's model, so the accuser here is our own vendor; weigh the attribution accordingly. EPOCH: the UAE's post-2013 campaign against the Muslim Brotherhood - designating it a terrorist organisation in 2014 and backing anti-Islamist forces from Egypt to Libya - now applied to Sudan, where Khartoum's army government cut diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi in 2025 over RSF support. CONSTRAINT: the Council has no enforcement power, so the stake is reputational and evidentiary - what goes into the record that later sanctions, arms-export decisions and court filings draw on. The International Court of Justice declined jurisdiction over Sudan's genocide case against the UAE in 2025, which leaves UN rapporteurs as one of the few standing channels. DESK: in Geneva, the OHCHR secretariat decides what testimony is received; in Washington and London, the desks that matter are the ones reviewing arms sales to the UAE. BASE RATE: platform takedown reports from Meta, OpenAI and others have named state-linked operations for years and almost never produced a government sanction against the state named; their usual effect is lost accounts and a citation. The attribution in reporting rests on Anthropic's assessment; its technical indicators have not been independently corroborated in the coverage. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: the UAE's formal response, OHCHR confirming it received the ghost-written submissions, or an independent research group matching the 300 accounts.

angles.effect: Pays in reputation at the Human Rights Council and in Western capitals weighing its role in Sudan; had sought to gain a record that recast accusers as Brotherhood-aligned
Gains a third-party document supporting its long charge that the UAE is a party to the war, useful in Geneva and in pressing arms-export reviews
Gains standing as a responsible platform ahead of AI regulation debates, and carries the risk of a state accusing a US company of political attribution
Pay twice - their names were borrowed, and real testimony now arrives at the UN under a cloud of suspicion

dec.kill: An independent researcher or the UN corroborating the accounts and submissions would upgrade this to confirmed; a detailed UAE rebuttal pointing to a non-state contractor, or Anthropic walking back 'high confidence', would downgrade the state link.

brief.head: House sets vote on bill letting Trump tariff buyers of Russian oil
brief.h: The House Rules Committee meets Monday on the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, passed 86-11 by the Senate, which lets the President impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on the five biggest buyers of Russian oil and gas - China and India lead that list - with a floor vote expected before members leave to campaign.
brief.t: This is not really a Russia bill, it is a bill about who pays for Russia's oil revenue. Moscow finances the war by selling crude at a discount to a handful of buyers; the Senate's answer is to threaten those buyers' entire export trade with the United States, a secondary tariff rather than a sanction on Russia itself. The catch is written into the text: the rate is 'up to' 100 per cent, and the President can waive it by certifying the national interest. So what the House is really voting on is whether to hand the White House a very large lever days before Xi Jinping's state visit - and three senior Democrats, Gregory Meeks, Richard Neal and Don Beyer, object precisely that it 'dramatically expands' presidential tariff power and could be turned on allies.
brief.context: EPOCH: a late chapter of the 1996 Iran and Libya Sanctions Act model, where Congress first punished third countries for doing business with a target, scaled up by CAATSA in 2017 - the last time Congress forced a Russia sanctions statute on a reluctant White House, 419-3 in the House. CONSTRAINT: Speaker Johnson needs near-unanimous Republican support on the procedural vote, and the House calendar before the midterms is short, so a slipped week can kill the bill for this Congress. DESK: after passage the operative desks are USTR on tariffs and Treasury's OFAC on the mandatory financial-institution sanctions; the waiver clause means the President's certification, not the statute, sets the real rate. MECHANISM: Daniel Drezner's sanctions paradox - threatened sanctions change behaviour more often than imposed ones, and a waivable threat is mainly a bargaining chip. BASE RATE: Senate-passed sanctions bills with veto-proof margins usually clear the House; the difference this time is a split majority on the procedural rule. We opened GEO-037 at 58 per cent that the House passes it by 31 October, and moved the US-China truce-collapse question up one point to 19 - the lever exists sooner, but a waiver is its likely first use. FALSIFIER: the rule fails on the floor or the vote is pulled without a new date.

consp.claim: That Lindsey Graham, the bill's author, did not die naturally - that he was killed shortly after returning from Ukraine to stop or, in other versions, to martyr and pass his Russia sanctions drive; posts have variously blamed Russia, Iran, Ukraine and Israel.
consp.spread: Began on X and among prominent MAGA commentators within hours of his death in July, documented by the Washington Post, PBS and Forbes; the Foundation for Defense of Democracies later tracked Russian state outlets amplifying it. It resurfaces whenever the renamed bill moves.
consp.read: The checkable facts run the other way: a preliminary medical examiner finding of a torn aorta after chest pains, reported by his office as a brief and sudden illness. The narrative is a textbook proportionality bias - a consequential bill and a sudden death must be connected - and its real effect is on the legislation, since the death is what the Senate cited as the final push to pass it.

watch: Monday's Oman meeting: who else stays away after Bahrain, at what level Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar attend, and whether any text mentions fees, permits or an administrator. Bahrain's 'no fees or permits' line is the benchmark to measure the outcome against.
Monday's House Rules Committee meeting on the Graham Act and the procedural vote after it - count Republican defections on the rule, not speeches.
Whether Iraq's three crossings with Iran reopen within a week with no named culprit (a message to Riyadh) or stay shut (Baghdad paying real trade to stay out of the target set).
The Kremlin on Miami: any confirmation that Putin will attend the 14-15 December G20, or a third-country venue offer, before Zelensky's late-September meeting with Trump.
The UAE's formal response to Anthropic's report, and whether OHCHR confirms receiving the ghost-written testimony at the Human Rights Council's 62nd session.
lesson: Today's lesson is a political-psychology one, and it is a tool for reading sabotage stories without being fooled in either direction: the PROPORTIONALITY BIAS. Psychologists studying conspiracy belief find that people expect big events to have big, intentional causes, so a sudden death or a string of explosions feels like it must be a plot - the correlational evidence for this is robust, though experiments isolating the exact trigger are weaker, so treat it as a tendency rather than a law. You can watch it on today's boards: an arms depot burns in Bulgaria and a train derails in Normandy on the same night, and within hours both are one campaign, or a Ukrainian false flag, or proof NATO is a paper tiger; the death of Senator Graham two months ago is still being tied to the sanctions bill the House votes on next week. The honest trap is that real covert campaigns also exist, so the fix is not to dismiss every plot but to ask the canon's test - does a RAIL predate the headline? For EMCO it does: Bulgarian prosecutors charged six Russians over earlier blasts at the same company and linked them to a named GRU unit. For the French derailment it does not yet: there is a rail fragment on the track and no attribution at all. What that predicts now is checkable: if the Bulgarian read is right, investigators will find ignition that storage failure cannot explain; if the fusion of the two stories were right, the French inquiry would turn up the same hand - and until it does, the disciplined position is two incidents, one with a history and one without.

quiz.q: Why would Baghdad close its own border crossings with Iran after drones launched from Iraq hit a Saudi pipeline?
options: Because Iran ordered Iraq to close them to protect the militias
To impose a visible cost on itself and show it is acting, so it does not become the target of US or Saudi retaliation
Because the drones were proven to have been driven through those crossings on the day of the attack
Because the crossings carry Saudi oil exports that needed protecting
quiz.why: Iraq cannot easily disarm the militias on its soil, so it punishes geography instead - closing gates and firing a commander. Paying a trade cost it controls is cheaper than a sanctions listing or a strike it doesn't.

quiz.q: The BRICS New Delhi declaration urged 'maximum restraint' but did not name Hormuz, the United States or Israel. What does that omission most likely tell you?
options: That BRICS members agree the war is over
That the text was written so that countries on opposite sides of the war, like Iran and the UAE, could both sign it
That China and India secretly support the US position
That the declaration is legally binding on its members
quiz.why: Consensus texts from mixed-alignment blocs trade specificity for signatures. The value is that Iran and the UAE stood on one page at all - not that the page commits anyone to anything.

quiz.q: The Graham sanctions bill lets the President impose tariffs of 'up to' 100 per cent on top buyers of Russian oil, with a national-interest waiver. What is the most accurate description of what the House would be handing the White House?
options: An automatic 100 per cent tariff on China and India within 30 days
A ban on all Russian oil imports into the United States
A large, adjustable lever whose actual rate and use depend on the President's own certification
A sanction that applies only to Russian companies
quiz.why: 'Up to' sets a ceiling, not a floor, and the waiver lets the President switch it off. Drezner's sanctions paradox says threats like this often do more work than the tariffs themselves - which is why the timing near Xi's visit matters.

quiz.q: Why does this desk treat the Bulgarian depot blast and the French train derailment differently, even though both are being called sabotage?
options: Because France is a bigger country than Bulgaria
Because the Bulgarian site belongs to a company whose earlier blasts led to charges against Russian intelligence officers, while the French case has no attribution or history yet
Because the French derailment caused no injuries
Because Bulgaria has already officially blamed Ukraine
quiz.why: A design read is allowed only when a rail predates the headline. EMCO has one - prior charges linked to GRU Unit 29155. The French case has a rail fragment on a track and nothing else, so fusing them is proportionality bias, not analysis.

quiz.q: A post reads: 'Iraq closing the border AND Iran asking for a joint investigation proves Iran is innocent.' Which observable would best test that claim?
options: Whether Iranian officials condemn the attack on television
Whether the recovered drone airframes and components trace to Iranian production or supply chains
Whether the price of Brent crude falls next week
Whether the BRICS declaration mentions Iraq
quiz.why: Joining an investigation is a cheap signal that a guilty and an innocent patron would both send - it also gives Tehran visibility into the findings. Forensics on the airframes separates the two; statements don't. Who gains from the 'innocence' framing: Tehran and the militia network. Who pays if it's wrong: Riyadh and the Iraqi border economy.

plumbing.epoch: E1, the 1973-79 rail on which oil was yoked to the dollar and Gulf surpluses were recycled into Treasuries, meeting E6, the 2019-21 plumbing-break-to-velocity-permit sequence still open in the form of an unended bill-buying programme. Today E1 was the one that moved, and a correction to yesterday's note belongs here: that security-for-barrels bargain is E1 in this module's numbering, not E4. Its unstated term was that the guarantor would keep the sea lanes open and would show up when a client was attacked. Both halves were tested inside thirty hours - the East-West pipeline shut, the Red Sea gate taken, and the guarantor declining a treaty partner's direct request for strikes twice while offering intelligence and targeting data instead. The old rail: a security guarantee underwritten by a navy with forward basing. The new permit: the guarantee is now explicitly partial - freedom of navigation for the lane, the land war behind it is the partner's problem - and the repricing that follows is denominated in hedging instruments rather than in barrels. DESIGN READ, gated and declined: no rail predates this. The refusal reads as drift and force-structure reality rather than as a plan to push Riyadh toward a hedge, and the incompetence alternative is straightforward - an administration that has said it will not start new wars discovering that its clients read that sentence as being about them.

sections.t: Saudi Arabia lost both of its roads around the Strait of Hormuz in thirty hours: drones from Iraq's Maysan province shut the East-West pipeline carrying four to five million barrels a day to Yanbu, and Houthi forces took Perim island at the mouth of Bab al-Mandab. Mohammed bin Salman asked Washington twice for strikes on the Houthis and was refused twice, receiving intelligence and targeting data instead.

The pipeline is not the story; the answer is. Since 1945 the bargain has been security for oil priced in dollars, on an unstated term: the guarantor defends the flow. Name the mechanism, the GUARANTEE LADDER - weapons, intelligence, escorts, and at the top, killing people who attack you. Clients assume they bought all of it; they bought only the rungs the guarantor's own interest will pay for. Riyadh reached for the top and was handed the third. Glenn Snyder's alliance security dilemma: a junior partner reads what its patron REFUSES more carefully than what it promises.

sections.h: Deep history I - when protection becomes tribute
sections.t: The oldest version of this ladder was built at Delos in 478 BC. The league was voluntary, aimed at Persia, and members could contribute ships or money. Most chose money, because money was convenient and crews were not. In 454 BC the treasury moved from Delos to Athens; phoros stopped meaning subscription and started meaning tribute, and some of it paid for the Parthenon. Thucydides records what became of members who tried to leave: Naxos around 470 and Thasos in 465 were besieged by the fleet they had helped finance. The guarantor prices the guarantee, and the price rises - but the sharper lesson is that the client's own convenience builds the cage. Those allies were disarmed by their preference for paying cash.

sections.h: Deep history II - real, and empty
sections.t: On 31 March 1939 Neville Chamberlain rose in the Commons and guaranteed Poland. It was formalised on 25 August as the Anglo-Polish Agreement of Mutual Assistance, carrying a secret protocol - published only after the war - that restricted the British obligation to aggression by Germany alone. So when the Red Army crossed on 17 September, Britain owed Poland precisely nothing. War was declared on 3 September; the French pushed a few miles into the Warndt forest and withdrew; Poland was finished in five weeks. The guarantee was legally genuine, publicly made and militarily undeliverable - honoured in declaration, void in relief, with the fine print written where the client could not read it.

sections.h: Deep history III - the hostage solution
sections.t: NATO was the attempt to fix that, and Article 5 repays reading slowly. Members assist by taking "such action as it deems necessary, including the use of armed force" - twelve lines where the Brussels Treaty's Article IV took four, because the US Senate would not sign automaticity. The famous clause is weaker than the clause it replaced. What made it hold for seventy-seven years was not text but Thomas Schelling's insight in Arms and Influence (1966): you cannot make a promise credible by asserting it, only by removing your own choice. American troops in West Germany and Korea, with their families, were no defence - at the Fulda Gap they would have been overrun in days. They were hostages, and a tripwire converts a future decision into an automatic consequence. Credibility bought with bodies, not adjectives. De Gaulle asked anyway - would Washington trade New York for Paris? - and answered himself with the force de frappe in 1960.

sections.h: Deep history IV - from the Quincy to Abqaiq
sections.t: On 14 February 1945, returning from Yalta, Roosevelt met Ibn Saud aboard the USS Quincy in the Great Bitter Lake. The ladder went up from there: the 1974 recycling arrangements; the Carter Doctrine of 23 January 1980, declaring an assault on the Gulf would be "repelled by any means necessary"; CENTCOM in 1983; half a million American soldiers deployed for a client state in 1991. The top rung was climbed exactly once. Then 14 September 2019: missiles and drones hit Abqaiq and Khurais and removed 5.7 million barrels a day, over half of Saudi production. The president said America was "locked and loaded," did nothing, and explained why in the sentence that has governed the Gulf ever since - that was an attack on Saudi Arabia, and it wasn't an attack on us. Seven years of Saudi behaviour follow: the Beijing-brokered normalisation with Tehran in 2023, and on 17 September 2025 the Saudi-Pakistan Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement, signed with a nuclear-armed state and left deliberately vague on whether the arsenal is included. Pakistan's defence minister said the capability "will be made available," then walked it back. The ambiguity is not sloppiness. It is the French move, performed by a client who has learned how credibility gets manufactured.

Guarantees decay from the top down: you stop striking before you stop deploying, and stop deploying before you stop selling. The rung that survives serves the guarantor's own interest - Washington kept the lane open, an American problem, and declined the land war behind it. Clients rarely defect; they dilute. Where it breaks: in 1939 Britain wanted to help and could not, in 2026 America can and will not.

Mearsheimer holds that commitments bind only where the guarantor's own survival is engaged; everything else is cheap talk - the logic of his 1993 case for Ukraine keeping its warheads. Ikenberry holds that institutionalised orders outlive the power that built them. Mearsheimer takes WHICH rungs held: the US defended the commons it consumes, not the war it doesn't. Ikenberry takes why there was no rupture: Riyadh took the intelligence and stayed. Then Schelling against Mearsheimer on the remedy - Article 5 has held over Estonia, where no American survival interest exists, because American battalions stand on it. Schelling wins the mechanism, Mearsheimer the forecast that nobody will station a tripwire in Yemen. Sagan supplies the falsifiable consequence: states build when someone else's guarantee loses credibility, not when the threat rises.

The US produces some 13.8 million barrels a day, and near eighty per cent of Hormuz crude goes to Asia: American hulls escort Chinese and Indian barrels. That subsidy to a rival will not survive twenty years of fiscal stress in a country whose debt service exceeds its defence budget - Kennedy's overstretch, or more precisely Gilpin's rising protection costs. By 2035 the American Gulf posture converts from insurance into a fee-and-arms business: about 60 per cent. Bolder: at least one Gulf state holds an overt or thinly-veiled latent nuclear capability by 2035, about 55 per cent. Our twelve-month ledger line on a Saudi announcement is 21 per cent, and a floor: hedging is covert, so watch reactor tenders for a fuel-cycle clause. Counterweight: announced after Suez and after Saigon too. Disconfirmers: US strikes on the Houthis within sixty days, or a ratified treaty with Riyadh.

Glenn Snyder, Alliance Politics (1997) - the abandonment-entrapment dilemma. - Thomas Schelling, Arms and Influence (1966), ch. 2-3 - why a tripwire beats a treaty. - Scott Sagan, "Why Do States Build Nuclear Weapons?" (International Security, 1996).
